projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Fink was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Robert L. Fink. Mr. Fink served in the US Army Air Corps with the 20th Air Force, 313th Bomb Wing, 505th Bomb Group, 482nd Squadron. He served in the Pacific Theater and his highest rank during World War II was captain. Mr. Fink was a prisoner of war. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Fink's home in Youngstown, Ohio on October 22, 2004. Robert was 84 at the time of this recording. Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Well, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living first?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ____+ where were you living at -- at that time?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: I was living in Austintown, on Raccoon Road. 162 Raccoon Road, as a matter of fact. That's where I grew up. And I was working for the Youngstown Sheet and Tube and on December the 6th I went to work at nine o'clock. I came home at -- on December the 7th at six o'clock in the morning and that's when I started hearing all the news then about the attack on Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: And it was quite scary because I knew where it was leave -- what it was leading to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. A. Previous to this time though I had been trying to get into the service. I was draft age, so I knew if I sat there eventually I would be drafted. So where I lived on Raccoon Road, right across this road from us -- we had a small farm -- but across the road from us was an airport. And I had watched these planes all my life come and go, come and go. And I never had been up in the air and I always had the urge to do it. So I thought, "Well, I'm going to try to get into the United States Army Air Force." And that's what I started out to do. And I started this in about 1940. And I went and I got an examination and I found out that they wouldn't pass me. I couldn't pass it because I had nose trouble. I -- I was only breathing through one side of my nose. They said, "Well, you've got to go and get a operation and then come back and we'll check you again." So that took care of 1940. I had to go get an operation and eventually I -- I got back to them and, oh, in the meantime, why, the draft board called me to come in. So I went in and I told them what I was doing and they said, "Well, okay you go ahead with it and keep us informed." So I did, and after the operation, why I contacted them again and then they sent me to Cleveland to get another examination. So I got the examination and they passed me. For a -- a physical exam, not a physical, but a mental. I can't think of what they call it, but anyway, you had to pass a test before you could qualify. And then in '41 I went and took that and then everything was set up. They said, "Well, we'll call you." Well, nobody called me and it come along to December the 7th and I thought, "Well, I'll hear from them now." And sure I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How soon after that did you hear?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: A couple days after that. It didn't take them long. They called and then on January -- January 19th of '42 I was called. I was to report to Columbus. Fort Hayes in Columbus, and that's where I started my Army Air Force career.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day at training?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Well, the first, yeah, the first day of training now, that took place in California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Well, the first -- the first day that I did any -- any -- any training was actually in Arizona, because I left Columbus after we joined and I went to Arizona to the base there. And they kept me there for a month and we had schooling there. Then they sent me to California -- Oxnard, California -- to flight training. And, yeah, that first -- that first trip -- flight in a plane was quite exciting, I'll tell you, because I had never been up in an airplane. And yeah, it was -- it was an exciting thing to happen. But that's where I took my initial training, was in Oxnard, California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: And, you know, for a farm boy from Ohio to get that far in just a few months, boy, that was quite exciting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a tough adjustment for you to be there, when you went into training with guys from all over the country? Was it hard to adjust to --?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, because they kept us busy. We were busy all the time and so you didn't have -- I didn't have any -- problems at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No problem getting along with the guys ___+?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, no problems. Well, the -- where -- where I was as a cadet in the Army Air Force, that's what all of them were, and they were all the same. We were sort of the same kind of -- everybody had an ambition. They were going to learn to fly, and most of them did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And everybody was there by choice probably?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: By choice, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what they wanted to do, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, you didn't get drafted and sent there. You--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: --you had to pick it out. And so that's -- that's where I got started. From Oxnard I went to Merced, California, which was another base, and that was more of advanced training. And then from Merced, I went to Victorville, California, which was out in the desert. And that was quite an experience, too, because we'd go out on the base, or on the -- on the edge of the runway to the planes and it would be 110 degrees. So they -- they -- were good to us that way, because we did most of our flying from like five o'clock in the morning till ten or eleven. Then they'd shut her down and we wouldn't go up again until maybe five or six o'clock in the evening, so we missed the center of the day there, because it was really too hot. Wasn't hot once you got in the air, but on the ground it was. And from -- from there, from Victorville, California, I graduated. And they gave us a choice as to where we wanted to go. And we could have gone into four-engine bombers, or twin-engine planes and -- or the transport, or the serve, or the training command. So I -- I -- I -- wanted the four-engine, but then I put down a second choice. I'm telling this because I thought it was kind of funny. The second choice was a twin-engine, and then they transport command, and I put the training command down as a last choice. So when they selected us, they said, "Now we're going to change the way, everything in the Air Force is done by the alphabet, but we're going to change that this time. We're going to start -- instead of starting with "A," -- we're going to start at the end of the alphabet. We're going to start with "Z." Well my name is Fink, "F," so I didn't get any of my choices. I ended up in the training command. So they sent me to Carlsbad, New Mexico -- which was a twin-engine bomber -- bombardier training command. So I started out there flying bombing missions in Mexico where you had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You -- you were a bombardier?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, no. I was a pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pilot, that's what I thought.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: And they -- they were -- they had targets set up around in the desert out there, and I guess we -- I -- for six months, that's what I did. And I'd take these bombardiers, these fellows what were doing the practicing, I'd fly them around there, and they'd drop bombs. And it was good training for them. They -- they were only with us like, a month, and then they were shipped off to Europe. Well, anyhow I -- about a -- I'll say six months -- they changed it into a navigation school. So then I started flying navigation students around and I flew all over the West out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Then, I don't know how this happened exactly, but they picked me out to be the base check pilot, so I didn't -- I stopped flying those things. And then I got all the -- the new graduates-- pilots that came in. I had to check each one of them, take them around, teach them how to fly the -- the plane. This was -- we had twin-engine planes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of planes?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: They were --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --a trainer?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: The trainers. They were known as AT-11 and AT-7.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, I'm guessing pilot was probably your first choice, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of your first solo flight during training?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah. The first solo flight, I had ten hours of instruction, and the - my -- my teacher said, "Well, I'm going send you up with a check pilot." And so I went with a check pilot, and he come back -- we come back, why, he got out and he said, "Well, he's all right. Let him solo. Let him go solo." And I -- that was that was quite a shock. I didn't know I was going to do it that quick. So I went and made the --I went through the procedure, took off, flew right-- we only flew right around the field once -- made a landing. And do you know, it was nice and smooth three-point landing from a distance. I didn't know I could do that. And even my instructor said, "Boy, that was a good landing." You know, I was by myself then. I was solo and the plane, when you take the -- those were small planes -- but when you take one person out of it, it changes the weight and it handles a little bit different then. I found that out, too. But I didn't have any trouble after that. I always was able to check out in these planes. By the way, Victorville was a twin-engine flying school. That's where I -- I -- it's funny, they -- when I was in the basic training, they sorted us out according to our height. All the shorter fellows went into the single-engine and all the tall fellows went into the double or two-engine so that's -- that's where I went. That's how I got in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Now -- now you want to -- want to go back to where --?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Go back -- go back to where you were talking about being a check pilot.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, I was a base check pilot and oh, that lasted for about a year, I guess it was there. And I had a lot of wild experiences. Some of those fellows weren't very good pilots. I was trying to check out, but we -- we didn't have any accidents. Everything come out all right. And then one day they put a notice on the bulletin board. Anyone with 1500 hours of first pilot time was eligible to fly B29's. And that was the -- the B-29 had just come out, and some of my buddies and I got together and we said, "You know, we should do that." And so then I -- I left the Carlsbad, New Mexico and I went to, oh, well anyhow, it was a four-engine base.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: And I learned to fly a B-17. So after the -- we got through with the B-17, I put in maybe a hundred hours in it, I guess. And then I went to Nebraska, and -- where the B29s were-- the B-29 base. And there I was checked out in a B-29 and I was there for, oh, a couple months, I guess. And then I -- then they put together a crew. I got a crew. There was 11 of us, and we-- we flew the B-17 the first couple weeks, and then we switched over to the 29. And then after we finished our training there, we went to -- and I can't think of the name -- another base in Nebraska, where we picked up a new, brand-new B-29 and headed for the -- for the West Coast. We took it and we went to California, and we had one -- one -- it was near San Francisco -- I can't think of the name of the base. You know, after 50 years, those -- those -- those things slip away from you. But anyhow, we had a rainy, real rainy weather. I was only there a couple of days and I thought, "Well, gee, they're not going to -- not going to -- send us out in this weather." And they said, "Sure. Come on, we're going tonight." And so I had to take off at night, 'cause I was going to fly to the Hawaiian Islands and they wanted us to take off at night so we would arrive there in the morning. And I got out on that runway -- I remember this -- and that rain was really coming down. "Well, well I guess we'll make it all right." And we did. We got off the ground, flew in the storm about halfway to Hawaii. And there's a -- there's a thing as Saint Elmo's Fire. I don't know whether you ever heard of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have heard of it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: But, it's -- it's a electric charge on the wings, and they'll run up and down the wings. Well, we ran into that the first time I ever saw it, and then it would jump from the plane to the clouds. And it just like lightning. And I thought, "Boy, I'm glad I'm on this end of it." But anyhow, that was an experience we had going to the Hawaiian Islands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Does it look like a lightning bolt or was it a ball of lightning?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Like a --like a ball. Maybe the edge of the wing will start to glow white and then they'll just run off. It's an electrical charge, is what it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: But anyhow that's -- that's how we got to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that when you went to Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: It was in December of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: I can't tell you exact date.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's okay. That's -- just gives me a rough idea of when you --.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, I, well, I probably left in November from California, because I got to the island of Tinian. I don't know whether you've heard of that or not. That's where the atomic bomb is -- were taken off from, and that's where I was headed for. And I stopped at the Hawaiian Islands, and there was another Johnston Island. We stopped there -- and these were refueling stops -- and then we went on into -- I went to Saipan, 'cause it was the only active base there. And I went into Saipan and they wouldn't let me stay there. They said, "No, you can't stay here." I was sent there, but because our planes are all out on bombing missions and when they come back this field is going to be full. So they sent me down to Guam. I went to Guam, that was the headquarters, that base, for the 20th Air Force. So I went down to Guam. And I got to Guam and we stayed one night. And the next day they said, "Well, Tinian has an -- has one of their runways finished. You go back up to Tinian today." So there was three of us there. There was, you know, three planes, and so we went back to Tinian. We took off, went to Tinian, and I was the third one in line. So the first one was the first -- first guy was the first one to ever land on that air base, and I was the third. But anyhow, we didn't we didn't do much of anything there for -- for the next month, because we were the first ones from the -- the squadron and the group actually to get out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your squadron?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: 482nd Squadron, 505th Bomb Group in the 20th Air Force. Well, there's another -- 313th Wing of the 20th Air Force. So we went -- we didn't do much for a couple of weeks and at Christmastime, came Christmas of '44, let's see, then the planes really started coming in. Then, you know, we were first ones to get there, but then they started filling up and we -- they'd been working on this field all the while we were there, and we hadn't been doing any flying, excepting the base commander wanted to go to the next island and around Tinian. You know, in -- he was stationed there on -- on Tinian, and he wanted to go to Saipan. And so he asked me if I would fly him. So my crew and I -- we didn't have anything else to do -- so we -- we flew the base commander. And he -- he made me get down and go close on these islands. He says, "I want to see if they're going -- there are any Japs there and if they're going to fire on us." I said, "Okay, if you want to do it, we'll do it." But we didn't get fired on, so there apparently wasn't any Japs left on 'em. But anyhow, in January we got our first mission. The crew and all the squadron had all arrived. Our first mission was on Iwo Jima. It was just before they invaded it. We went up there and a dropped a lot of bombs on, and bombed, but-- but later on, we found out that the bombs we dropped didn't do any good, because the Japs were in tunnels. They were deep in the -- they were deep in the island. Oh, we may have damaged some things, but it didn't do much good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any opposition on that mission any --?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --___+force at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, we had -- we had a couple of more missions. And I can't think of the name of the island -- one of the islands that was captured by the Japanese -- that we bombed and that was two or three times. So anyhow, to make a long story short -- I'm coming to the end of my career here in a hurry -- I-- I was going to get, well, the crew on the -- on the -- down on the -- our -- our-- our base where we lived, was about a mile from the runways. So on the way there, one of the squadron commanders saw a bunch of oil drums and he said we ought to take those down because we could use them. The Japs had left them there. So we were -- I got in a jeep with him. I was going down to the base -- I wasn't worrying about the oil drums -- and he said, "I'm going to stop and see them." So he stopped and he went over and looked around and he motioned to us, "Come on over." So I walked over there and all over ground was spaghetti, looked like, but it wasn't. It was it was pow -- it was -- that's, gun powder. Gun powder, that's what I'm trying to say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, and this had been a gun -- in Japanese gun place -- out there and I don't know what happened next, but it exploded and I got burned. I -- it was behind me and I had my sleeves rolled up, so I got both arms burned, third-degree burns. And the other fellow, one other fellow, got -- got bad burns. And it was two other ones that just happened to be far enough away, they didn't get anything. Now, they -- they said it was a -- a mine. A land mine. Somehow I don't believe that, because it was just fire, is all. Some reason or another we set that thing on fire. And I, to this day, I don't know. The other fellows, they don't know either what happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: The guard came by one day and said the Americans had dropped a bomb, a big bomb. And he says one bomb -- one city gone. Well, I don't know what the hell he's talking about, but he - he got his point across. And this was, I think it was on the 9th, and then on the 15th is when they told us they're going to move us out of the cell -- that the War was over, and maybe they dropped a second bomb then, too, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Oh, I -- it was real, real, well, really exciting. I landed in New Philadelphia, Ohio. There was a -- they had a --the Army had a hospital there and they flew us from California and landed me in New Philadelphia. And I knew it was going happen and I called my parents and told them I'd be in New Philadelphia and they could pick me up there. And sure enough, when I got there, they took me inside and it wasn't very long, here comes my mother and father. They came down and picked me up and they released me right then and there was no arguing about it. So I -- that's how I got home. They brought me home here to Austintown and, of course, the whole family was glad to see me and, oh, I had lot of relatives. And they all came down to visit me and I had to tell them all my story. And that -- that about concludes what.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What happened to the rest of your crew that bailed out?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: The -- two of them were killed, now--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After they got to the ground or killed ___+?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, they were killed in the plane. Now, whether they -- they were hit. You know, there was bullets flew in that plane. Whether they got hit or what happened, I'm not sure, no. No one ever will know and, you know, when we had a fire in the number three engine and I knew the wing would come off, wouldn't be too long. And sure enough, the fellow that was the bombardier, he stayed in the service and he went back to Japan and he found the airplane and he said the wing was off it. The wing was gone and they -- the Japanese showed him where found -- and they -- the Japs showed him where the wing was, and it was a like a half a mile away. So it did come off. And there was two -- two fellows -- two of the crew was killed and they were buried there in Japan. And, of course, they dug them up and brought them back. They're buried in Hawaiian Islands now, but the rest of the crew all survived.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they all captured?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: They were all captured, yeah. Now, I didn't know, but they were -- there was three or four of them up in the first cell and I was down in the sixth cell. And all that time I didn't know they were in there. There's no way to communicate. And I didn't find out until we got out on in the camp in Aomori and here they are. I said, "Hey, I seen you guys before," but--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any parcels at all when you were a prisoner? A.: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't cooperate with that--?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --did they?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, we didn't get anything. We were just fortunate to get enough rice to keep us alive.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of -- of close buddies either before or after you were shot down? Particularly close buddies from that time?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Because the -- the amount of time that I spent with anyone was always short. I never was, you know, I left with the crew, but I was separated from the crew within a month or two months there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many missions did you fly before you were ___+?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: I just -- I just -- I thought I had six.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: But my record shows only two.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: So, they didn't count these ones that I we were flying on the islands. I guess 'cause nobody shot at us. So I--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then when you came back, was that the first mission that you were on after you came back?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: That, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was ___+, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, this crew that I was with had flown 15 missions. This was going to be their 16th, so they only made 15 and a half. I don't--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before -- before you were shot down, do you have any memories of mail call? Were you dating or were you just a single guy at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: I was a single guy, yeah, so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mail call from family or anything like that that? Not a whole lot?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: No, I didn't get much mail out there. I -- I didn't know her at the time. I didn't meet her until after the War, and I didn't have any steady girlfriends or anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of that time does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind? You certainly shared a lot of vivid memories, but does anything else that we didn't - that I didn't ask you about? WOMAN: ___+ disease in your camp,

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The disease in your camp? WOMAN: Mice and diarrhea.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Oh, yeah well--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Conditions?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Oh, the conditions were terrible. We -- we had a -- in the corner of the cell, there was a hole in the floor. That was the toilet. Course, we didn't make many trips there because we weren't eating anything, you know, a little, little bit of rice. You'd go a week without having a bowel movement, just to show you how much it amounted to. It didn't amount to much of anything. Enough to keep you alive is about all. But, yeah, we had lice in there. Well, I was living in a stall, is what I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they keep -- was it possible they kept the guys in the grounds in the Imperial Palace so that basically the prisoners would be safe from air raids?

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 'Cause I know I've heard that that we were restricted--

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --not supposed to bomb the Palace.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, we were told not to bomb the Palace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Keeping you as possible hostages or whatever.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, well that might -- that might have been what it was all about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Because the stories that we used to hear, and that I -- I believed, is that the ones that went down where they were bombing like on --on the edge of the city, or in the city, most of the people got killed or most of them got killed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: They said -- I read statistics that said that 65% of the people that we lost over there were the 20th Air Force. Never came back. They were all dead. So that's only 35 percent of us got out of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: And it was probably the fact that it was so late in the War. They -- Japanese - were having second thoughts about what they should be doing. That's what I figure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Well, and apparently having second thoughts on that moment they tied you up on the pole.

sp.speaker: Robert Fink
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, I -- I -- I don't know what that was all about, but it had all the earmarks of being an execution and the fact that they didn't do it, I'm glad they didn't. But, well.

sp.p: Very good. You think that it covers it?
